patient.name: Maureen Gallagher
patient.complaint: Left lower abdominal pain and fever for 2 days
background: Chronic constipation for years; low-fibre diet
Previous milder left-sided cramps and bloating that settled
Hypertension on amlodipine; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older patient, LIF pain, fever and raised CRP, or a complication clue such as pneumaturia, a tender LIF mass or generalised peritonism.

points: Maureen, 67, has **constant left iliac fossa pain** for 2 days.
Worse on moving; she feels hot and has gone off her food.
Some loose stools, now constipated again; mild nausea.
No rectal bleeding, no weight loss, no urinary symptoms.

visual.title: Where Maureen's pain is
visual.caption: LIF pain in an older patient: think sigmoid diverticular disease first. RIF pain points to appendicitis instead.

steps.lead: Maureen almost certainly has **sigmoid diverticula**. The question is which stage: just present, causing symptoms, or inflamed.

steps.title: Three words, three stages
head: Feature
Diverticulosis
Diverticular disease
Diverticulitis
rows: LIF pain, bloating, bowel habit change

steps.lead: Years of **constipation**, a low-fibre diet, obesity, little exercise and age over 60: Maureen ticks every box.

points: Her earlier episodes: cramps and bloating, no fever, settled alone.
Today: **localised LIF tenderness and guarding**, no generalised rigidity.
Bowel sounds present; no hernias; rectal exam soft stool.
She looks unwell but is not peritonitic.

steps.lead: Her old episodes were **diverticular disease**; today's fever, tachycardia and localised tenderness make this **acute diverticulitis**.

steps.q: Maureen has 2 days of LIF pain, fever 38.4°C and localised LIF guarding. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Fever plus localised LIF tenderness in an older patient is **diverticulitis**. Diverticulosis is asymptomatic; volvulus gives massive distension and absolute constipation.

steps.lead: Maureen's guarding is **localised**. Rigidity, rebound and a systemically unwell patient would mean **perforation with peritonitis**.
Ask Maureen about **air or faeces in her urine** and recurrent UTIs. Watch for worsening pain, sepsis or a palpable mass: complicated disease.

steps.text: **Pneumaturia + faecaluria + recurrent UTIs** in someone with diverticular disease = **colovesical fistula**. Diagnose with cystoscopy/cystography; it needs surgical repair.
LIF pain with **weight loss, rectal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia** is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. Do not let 'probable diverticular disease' stop the later colonoscopy.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast) or a timing question where colonoscopy is wrong acutely and right once inflammation has settled.

steps.lead: Maureen's **FBC, CRP and U&Es** show how inflamed and how dry she is.

steps.title: Maureen's bloods on arrival
steps.text: Neutrophilia and a CRP of 168 fit diverticulitis. A high urea says she needs fluids.

visual.title: Maureen's CRP
visual.label: Maureen 168
visual.caption: A CRP above about 150 raises the chance of complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation), so she needs imaging.

steps.q: Which investigation best confirms diverticulitis and looks for complications?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
steps.r: **CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast** is the gold standard. Colonoscopy is dangerous while the bowel is inflamed.

steps.lead: Maureen's fever and high CRP earn her a **contrast CT**: it confirms diverticulitis and looks for abscess or free gas.

points: CT: **thickened sigmoid wall** with pericolic fat stranding.
A **4 cm pericolic abscess** beside the sigmoid.
No free gas; no obstruction; bladder normal.

steps.text: Never scope acute diverticulitis. **Colonoscopy** (or air insufflation) can **perforate** the inflamed bowel. Image with CT now, scope later.

steps.lead: Maureen's **colonoscopy** is booked once the inflammation has settled, to exclude a cancer hiding behind the inflamed segment.

visual.title: When to scope
visual.label: Maureen at 7 weeks
visual.caption: Colonoscopy is usually done around 6 weeks after recovery.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where severity decides: fibre for diverticular disease, oral co-amoxiclav for mild diverticulitis, admission with IV antibiotics when unwell, drainage for an abscess, Hartmann's for perforation.

steps.title: Match the treatment to the stage
nodes: Diverticular disease → fibre, fluids, treat constipation
Mild diverticulitis, well → analgesia, fluids, ± oral co-amoxiclav, safety-net
Unwell or complicated → admit, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, surgical review
steps.caption: Each rung up the ladder is a sicker patient.

steps.lead: Had Maureen been well with mild pain, she would go home on **analgesia, fluids** and, if indicated, **oral co-amoxiclav**, with safety-netting.

steps.q: Maureen is febrile, HR 102, with a 4 cm abscess on CT. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Admit for IV antibiotics and IV fluids
steps.r: Unwell with complicated diverticulitis: **admit, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, surgical review**. She is not peritonitic, so no emergency laparotomy.

steps.lead: Maureen is managed as an **acute surgical admission**: IV antibiotics, IV fluids and a surgical review.
Maureen's 4 cm abscess is **drained under CT guidance**. Hartmann's would be needed only if she perforated with peritonitis.

visual.title: Maureen's response to treatment
visual.caption: CRP peaks on day 1, then falls after drainage and IV antibiotics. A rising CRP or swinging fever would mean an undrained collection.

steps.text: **Hartmann's procedure**: resect the diseased sigmoid, bring out an **end colostomy** and close the rectal stump. Reversal is considered months later.

steps.lead: Maureen's plan follows **NICE** guidance on diverticular disease and the acute abdomen.

points: Day 5: switched to **oral co-amoxiclav** to finish the course.
Advice: high-fibre diet, plenty of fluids, treat constipation.
Return if pain worsens, fever returns or urine changes.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why diverticula form where vasa recta pierce the wall, why the sigmoid is affected, or how a complication arises.

steps.lead: Maureen's straining over years raised the pressure in her **sigmoid**, pushing mucosa out where the **vasa recta** pierce the muscle.

steps.title: How a diverticulum forms
nodes: High intraluminal pressure, highest in the sigmoid
Mucosa and submucosa herniate where vasa recta pierce the muscularis

steps.q: Why is the sigmoid colon the commonest site?
o: It has the highest intraluminal pressure
It has the most lymphoid tissue
It has the poorest blood supply
steps.r: The narrow sigmoid generates the **highest intraluminal pressures**, so mucosa herniates there.

steps.text: Colonic diverticula are **false (pulsion) diverticula**: only mucosa and submucosa push out, not the full muscular wall.

steps.lead: A **faecolith** likely blocked one of Maureen's diverticula; bacteria overgrew and a micro-perforation walled off as her **abscess**.

steps.title: From blocked pouch to complication
nodes: Repeated inflammation → fibrosis → stricture → large bowel obstruction

steps.text: **Co-amoxiclav** is chosen because colonic flora are **Gram-negative** (e.g. E. coli) and **anaerobic** (e.g. Bacteroides).

mcq.q: Which term means diverticula are present but cause no symptoms?
mcq.r: **Diverticulosis** is the asymptomatic presence of diverticula; diverticular disease means they cause symptoms.

mcq.q: Which part of the colon is most commonly affected by diverticula?
mcq.r: The **sigmoid**, where intraluminal pressure is highest. The rectum is spared.

mcq.q: Which is the key driver of diverticular formation?
mcq.r: **Chronic constipation** with a low-fibre diet raises intraluminal pressure.

mcq.q: Pneumaturia and recurrent UTIs in a patient with diverticular disease suggest which complication?
mcq.r: **Colovesical fistula**: gas and faeces track from colon to bladder.

mcq.q: Which is the gold-standard investigation in suspected acute diverticulitis?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
mcq.r: **Contrast CT** shows sigmoid wall thickening, fat stranding, abscess or free gas.

mcq.q: Why is colonoscopy avoided during acute diverticulitis?
o: It risks perforating the inflamed bowel
mcq.r: The inflamed wall can **perforate**; scope later to exclude malignancy.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is first-line for diverticulitis in the notes?
mcq.r: **Co-amoxiclav** covers Gram-negative and anaerobic gut flora.

mcq.q: How is a diverticular abscess managed?
Which operation is used for perforated diverticulitis with peritonitis?
mcq.r: **Hartmann's**: sigmoid resection, end colostomy, rectal stump closed.

mcq.q: Where in the colonic wall do diverticula form?
o: Between the taeniae and the mesentery at random
Where the vasa recta penetrate the muscularis
mcq.r: They herniate through weak points where the **vasa recta** pierce the muscularis propria.

prompts.q: Define diverticula, diverticulosis, diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem's symptoms decide which word is the answer.

points.p: Diverticula: outpouchings of the bowel wall, mostly sigmoid colon
points.why: The sigmoid has the highest intraluminal pressure.

points.p: Diverticulosis: diverticula present, no symptoms
points.why: Often found on colonoscopy or CT done for another reason.

points.p: Diverticular disease: diverticula causing symptoms (pain, bloating, bowel change)
points.why: No fever or major CRP rise.

points.p: Diverticulitis: inflammation or infection of diverticula
points.why: Fever, raised WCC and CRP point to it.

prompts.q: Who gets diverticular disease? Name the risk factors.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem hides the risk factor in the social history.

points.p: Low-fibre diet
points.why: Small hard stools raise intraluminal pressure.

points.p: Chronic constipation (key driver)
points.why: The notes call constipation the key driver.

points.p: Obesity and sedentary lifestyle
points.why: Both are listed risk factors.

points.p: Age over 60
points.why: LIF pain in an older patient is the classic stem.

prompts.q: What is the classic presentation of acute diverticulitis, and what suggests perforation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: LIF is the 'left-sided appendicitis'; peritonism means it has perforated.

points.p: Acute LIF pain and tenderness
points.why: RIF pain points to appendicitis instead.

points.p: Fever with raised WCC and CRP
points.why: Fever separates diverticulitis from diverticular disease.

points.p: Loss of appetite, nausea, change in bowel habit
points.why: Often alternating diarrhoea and constipation.

points.p: Perforation: systemically unwell with rigidity, guarding and rebound (peritonitis)
points.why: Generalised peritonism means free perforation.

prompts.q: List the complications of diverticulitis and how each presents.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each complication has one tell-tale clue.

points.p: Abscess: swinging fever, tender LIF mass
points.why: Suspect if not improving on antibiotics.

points.p: Perforation and peritonitis
points.why: Free gas on erect CXR or CT.

points.p: Fistula, especially colovesical
points.why: Pneumaturia, faecaluria, recurrent UTI.

points.p: Stricture causing bowel obstruction
points.why: Repeated inflammation and fibrosis narrow the sigmoid.

prompts.q: What are the features of a colovesical fistula and how is it diagnosed and treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: gas or faeces in the urine is pathognomonic.

points.p: Pneumaturia (air in urine)
points.why: The single most specific clue.

points.p: Faecaluria
points.why: Debris in the urine.

points.p: Recurrent UTIs
points.why: Often mixed gut organisms.

points.p: Diagnosed by cystoscopy/cystography; needs surgical repair
points.why: Will not heal with antibiotics alone.

prompts.q: What are the first-line tests and the gold-standard investigation in suspected diverticulitis, and what does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CT is the answer for 'diagnostic'; bloods for 'initial'.

points.p: Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&Es
points.why: Raised WCC and CRP support inflammation; urea shows dehydration.

points.p: Gold standard: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
points.why: Also finds abscess, perforation or fistula.

points.p: Shows sigmoid wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding
points.why: Free gas or a collection means complicated disease.

prompts.q: When is colonoscopy done in diverticulitis, and why not earlier?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'urgent colonoscopy' is a classic wrong option in the acute phase.

points.p: Later, once acute inflammation has settled (about 6 weeks)
points.why: Timing is the whole question.

points.p: To exclude malignancy or other pathology
points.why: Colorectal cancer can mimic or coexist with diverticular disease.

points.p: Avoided acutely: high risk of perforating the inflamed bowel
points.why: Insufflation and the scope stress the inflamed wall.

prompts.q: How do you manage diverticular disease, mild diverticulitis and severe diverticulitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: read the observations first; how unwell the patient is decides home versus admission.

points.p: Diverticular disease: increase dietary fibre, hydration, manage constipation
points.why: Lifestyle advice is first-line.

points.p: Mild uncomplicated diverticulitis: analgesia, fluids, safety-netting
points.why: Many well patients are managed at home.

points.p: Oral co-amoxiclav if antibiotics indicated
points.why: Covers Gram-negative and anaerobic gut flora.

points.p: Severe/unwell: admit, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, surgical review
points.why: Complicated disease is an acute abdomen emergency.

prompts.q: What is the definitive treatment for a diverticular abscess, a perforation and a stricture?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match each complication to its procedure.

points.p: Abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage
points.why: Plus IV antibiotics; surgery only if drainage fails.

points.p: Severe/perforated: Hartmann's procedure
points.why: Sigmoid resection with end colostomy.

points.p: Stricture: laparotomy
points.why: A stricture causes large bowel obstruction.

prompts.q: Why do diverticula form, and why mostly in the sigmoid colon?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pressure plus a weak point.

points.p: Weak points where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria
points.why: Mucosa and submucosa herniate through these gaps.

points.p: Sigmoid has the highest intraluminal pressure
points.why: Hence sigmoid and LIF predominance.

points.p: Constipation and low-fibre diet raise pressure and straining
points.why: The modifiable driver.

points.p: Mucosa/submucosa herniate (false diverticula)
points.why: No muscle layer in the wall of the pouch.

prompts.q: Why does diverticulitis develop, and how do its complications arise?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one blocked pouch explains every complication.

points.p: A faecolith obstructs a diverticulum
points.why: Like appendicitis in miniature.

points.p: Bacterial overgrowth, inflammation and micro-/macro-perforation
points.why: Micro-perforation is contained; macro-perforation is free.

points.p: Localised perforation → abscess; erosion into bladder → colovesical fistula
points.why: The bladder lies next to the sigmoid.

points.p: Free perforation → faeculent peritonitis; fibrosis → stricture → obstruction
points.why: Stricture is a cause of large bowel obstruction.

glossary.diverticula: Small outpouchings of the bowel wall, usually in the sigmoid colon.
glossary.diverticulum: A single outpouching of the bowel wall.
glossary.diverticulosis: Diverticula are present but cause no symptoms.
glossary.diverticular disease: Diverticula that cause symptoms such as pain, bloating or bowel habit change.
glossary.diverticulitis: Inflammation or infection of one or more diverticula, with fever and raised inflammatory markers.
glossary.sigmoid colon: The S-shaped last part of the colon before the rectum, in the left iliac fossa.
glossary.LIF: Left iliac fossa: the left lower part of the abdomen.
glossary.peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rigidity, rebound and pain on movement.
glossary.peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, usually from infection or perforation; a surgical emergency.
glossary.guarding: Involuntary tensing of the abdominal muscles when the inflamed area is pressed.
glossary.rebound tenderness: Pain worse when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released; a sign of peritonitis.
glossary.rigidity: A board-like abdomen from constant muscle spasm; suggests generalised peritonitis.
glossary.colovesical fistula: An abnormal connection between the colon and the bladder.
glossary.fistula: An abnormal connection between two hollow organs or an organ and the skin.
glossary.pneumaturia: Passing gas bubbles in the urine.
glossary.cystoscopy: Looking inside the bladder with a camera passed up the urethra.
glossary.cystography: X-ray of the bladder after filling it with contrast, to show leaks or fistulas.
glossary.stricture: An abnormal narrowing of a tube such as the bowel, often from scarring.
glossary.fat stranding: Hazy streaks in the fat on CT, showing inflammation next to the bowel.
glossary.faecolith: A hard stone of compacted faeces that can block a diverticulum or the appendix.
glossary.vasa recta: Small straight arteries that pierce the colonic muscle to supply the mucosa.
glossary.muscularis propria: The main muscle layer of the bowel wall.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; covers Gram-negative and anaerobic gut bacteria.
glossary.Hartmann's procedure: Sigmoid resection with an end colostomy and a closed rectal stump.
glossary.end colostomy: The cut end of the colon brought out onto the abdominal wall as a stoma.
glossary.percutaneous drainage: Draining a collection with a tube placed through the skin under image guidance.
glossary.laparotomy: An open operation through a large incision in the abdominal wall.
glossary.colonoscopy: A camera examination of the whole colon, passed through the anus.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: a blood marker that rises with inflammation or infection.
glossary.WCC: White cell count; raised in infection and inflammation.
glossary.Hartmann's: Short for Hartmann's procedure: sigmoid resection with an end colostomy.
glossary.safety-netting: Telling a patient which symptoms mean they should seek help again, and how.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a 3 day history of constant left lower abdominal pain and loose stools. He has had chronic constipation for years. He has lost his appetite. His temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. He is tender with guarding in the left iliac fossa only. There is no rectal bleeding and no weight loss.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about lower abdominal pain: the side of the pain and the fever narrow it fast.

clues: guarding in the left iliac fossa only
no rectal bleeding and no weight loss
steps.x: Older, constipated, LIF pain, fever and localised guarding, raised WCC and CRP: inflamed sigmoid diverticula.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Older patient + LIF pain + fever + raised CRP = **diverticulitis**.

elim: Appendicitis gives RIF pain, usually in younger patients.
Carcinoma gives weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, not acute fever.
Ischaemic colitis gives sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea in a vasculopath.
Volvulus gives massive distension and absolute constipation.

steps.x: **C. Diverticulitis.** Rule: LIF pain + fever in the over-60s is diverticulitis until CT says otherwise.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 2 day history of left iliac fossa pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. She is tender with guarding in the left iliac fossa. There is no generalised rigidity. She has had similar milder episodes before.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' means the test that confirms it and shows complications.

clues: left iliac fossa pain and fever
steps.x: Febrile, tachycardic, very high CRP: suspected complicated diverticulitis needing cross-sectional imaging.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast** is the gold standard.

elim: AXR shows obstruction or gross free gas only; it cannot show diverticulitis.
Barium enema is not used acutely and risks barium peritonitis.
Colonoscopy may perforate the inflamed bowel; do it later.
Ultrasound cannot reliably assess the sigmoid or a deep abscess.

steps.x: **D. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.** Rule: CT now, colonoscopy later.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man was admitted 3 days ago with diverticulitis and started on IV antibiotics. He still has a swinging fever and a tender left iliac fossa mass. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. His abdomen is soft away from the mass. CT shows a 5 cm pericolic abscess with no free gas.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step: he is already on IV antibiotics, so what treats the specific complication?

clues: 5 cm pericolic abscess with no free gas
steps.x: A contained abscess not settling on antibiotics, without peritonitis or free gas.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drain the pus: **CT-guided percutaneous drainage**.

elim: Hartmann's is for perforation with peritonitis; there is no free gas.
He is septic with a collection; he cannot go home.
Total colectomy is far too radical for sigmoid disease.
Colonoscopy risks perforation acutely.

steps.x: **A. CT-guided percutaneous drainage.** Rule: abscess = drain; free perforation = Hartmann's.

technique.stem: A 72 year old woman has a CT scan showing many small outpouchings of the sigmoid colon. She has eaten a low-fibre diet and been constipated for decades. The pouches lie in rows along the colonic wall, between the taeniae coli.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of their formation?
o: Congenital full-thickness outpouching of the wall
Herniation of mucosa where vasa recta penetrate the muscle
Ischaemia of the watershed splenic flexure
Twisting of the sigmoid on its mesentery

steps.x: Mechanism of diverticula: think pressure and weak points.

clues: lie in rows along the colonic wall
steps.x: High pressure from constipation; regular rows match where blood vessels pierce the wall.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mucosa and submucosa **herniate through gaps where the vasa recta penetrate** the muscularis propria.

elim: Congenital full-thickness pouch describes a true diverticulum such as Meckel's.
Watershed ischaemia causes ischaemic colitis, not pouches.
Transmural granulomas are Crohn's disease.
Twisting is sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: acquired, false, pulsion diverticula at vasa recta entry points.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 2 day history of constant left lower abdominal pain and nausea. She has lost her appetite. She has long-standing constipation and is obese. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. She is tender in the left iliac fossa with localised guarding. There is no rectal bleeding.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, localised LIF tenderness and raised inflammatory markers in an older, constipated woman is diverticulitis. Appendicitis is right-sided; IBS has no fever or raised CRP.

steps.x: Diagnosis: use the pain site, age and fever.
Older, risk factors, LIF pain, fever and localised peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Diverticulitis.**

elim: Appendicitis is RIF and usually younger.
IBS never causes fever or a raised CRP.
Ischaemic colitis presents with bloody diarrhoea.
Volvulus causes gross distension and absolute constipation.

steps.x: **B. Diverticulitis.** Rule: the 'left-sided appendicitis' of older adults.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has had three urinary tract infections in 4 months. He has noticed bubbles in his urine when passing it and, once, brown debris. He had an episode of diverticulitis treated with antibiotics last year. He is otherwise well. Urine culture has grown mixed coliforms.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent mixed-coliform UTIs after diverticulitis mean a colovesical fistula. Emphysematous cystitis causes gas but not faecal debris.

steps.x: Diagnosis of recurrent UTIs: look for a gut source.

clues: three urinary tract infections in 4 months
steps.x: Pneumaturia, faecaluria, recurrent UTI and previous diverticulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colovesical fistula**, a complication of diverticulitis.

elim: Bladder cancer presents with painless haematuria.
Prostatitis gives perineal pain, no gas or faeces.
Emphysematous cystitis is a diabetic infection; no faecal debris.
Stricture causes poor stream, not pneumaturia.

steps.x: **C. Colovesical fistula.** Rule: pneumaturia + faecaluria = fistula.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with known diverticular disease has 1 day of left iliac fossa pain that has spread across his whole abdomen. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness throughout. An erect chest X-ray is performed (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: LIF pain spreading to generalised peritonitis with free gas in a man with known diverticular disease is perforated diverticulitis. A perforated duodenal ulcer starts in the epigastrium.

steps.x: Diagnosis with an X-ray: free gas means a perforated viscus; the history says which one.

clues: left iliac fossa pain that has spread
steps.x: Started in the LIF, now generalised peritonitis and shock; free air under the diaphragm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated diverticulitis** with faeculent peritonitis.

elim: Pancreatitis does not cause free intraperitoneal gas.
Ischaemic colitis gives bloody diarrhoea, not free gas early.
Duodenal ulcer pain starts in the epigastrium, often with NSAID use.
Ruptured AAA causes back pain and shock, not free gas.

steps.x: **C. Perforated diverticulitis.** Rule: the starting site of the pain tells you which organ perforated.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 6 month history of intermittent left lower abdominal cramps, bloating and alternating constipation and loose stools. She has no weight loss or rectal bleeding. A colonoscopy last month showed multiple sigmoid diverticula and no other abnormality. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Her left iliac fossa is mildly tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Symptomatic diverticula without fever or a major CRP rise is diverticular disease. Diverticulosis is asymptomatic; diverticulitis needs inflammation.

steps.x: A terminology question in disguise: symptoms, but is there inflammation?

clues: intermittent left lower abdominal cramps, bloating
multiple sigmoid diverticula and no other abnormality
steps.x: Symptoms are present, but no fever and only a trivial CRP: no active inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diverticula causing symptoms = **diverticular disease**.

elim: Diverticulitis needs fever and raised inflammatory markers.
Diverticulosis is the asymptomatic state; she has symptoms.
New IBS over 60 is unlikely, and diverticula explain it.
UC gives bloody diarrhoea and an inflamed mucosa on colonoscopy.

steps.x: **A. Diverticular disease.** Rule: -osis = none, disease = symptoms, -itis = inflamed.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman is on day 5 of IV antibiotics for diverticulitis. She has a swinging fever and worsening left iliac fossa pain. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. There is a tender mass in the left iliac fossa. The rest of her abdomen is soft.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: A swinging fever and tender LIF mass despite antibiotics is a pericolic abscess. Faecal peritonitis would cause generalised rigidity.

steps.x: Which complication: match the clinical clue to it.

clues: tender mass in the left iliac fossa
rest of her abdomen is soft
steps.x: Not settling, swinging fever, localised mass, no generalised peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pus collecting next to the sigmoid: **pericolic abscess**.

elim: A fistula causes pneumaturia and UTIs.
A stricture causes obstructive symptoms over time.
Faecal peritonitis gives a rigid abdomen and shock.
No distension, vomiting or absolute constipation.

steps.x: **E. Pericolic abscess.** Rule: swinging fever + mass = abscess, which needs drainage.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man has a 2 day history of left iliac fossa pain and fever. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 94 bpm. He is tender with localised guarding in the left iliac fossa. A CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is requested to confirm the suspected diagnosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT?
o: Coffee bean sign arising from the pelvis
Dilated small bowel loops with a transition point
Sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding
Target sign in the right colon
practice.e: Acute diverticulitis shows sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding on CT. Thumbprinting suggests ischaemia; coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: A finding question: first name the diagnosis, then its CT sign.

clues: left iliac fossa pain and fever
localised guarding in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Classic acute diverticulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thickened sigmoid wall and pericolic fat stranding.**

elim: Coffee bean is a sigmoid volvulus sign on AXR.
Dilated small bowel with transition point is small bowel obstruction.
A target sign suggests intussusception.
Thumbprinting at the splenic flexure suggests ischaemic colitis.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: inflammation on CT = wall thickening + fat stranding.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has a 3 day history of left iliac fossa pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. She is tender with guarding in the left iliac fossa. There is no generalised peritonism.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
practice.e: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast confirms diverticulitis and detects abscess or perforation. Colonoscopy is avoided acutely because of perforation risk.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' = the gold-standard test.

clues: left iliac fossa pain and fever
steps.x: Suspected diverticulitis, CRP 176: look for complications.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.**

elim: Ultrasound is poor for the sigmoid and deep collections.
AXR cannot show diverticulitis.
Colonoscopy risks perforation acutely.
Erect CXR looks only for free gas; she is not peritonitic.

steps.x: **D. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.**

practice.stem: A 61 year old man was treated for CT-confirmed acute diverticulitis 2 weeks ago. He has now completed his antibiotics and his pain has resolved. He is eating normally. He has never had any colonic investigation. He asks whether he needs any further tests.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Colonoscopy is done once the inflammation has settled, to exclude malignancy. Scoping early risks perforation; doing nothing could miss a cancer.

steps.x: Follow-up investigation after an attack: think about what could be hiding.
Recovered, but the colon has never been seen; 2 weeks is still early.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colonoscopy once inflammation has settled** (around 6 weeks) to exclude cancer.

elim: CT colonography inflates the colon; too soon, and cannot biopsy.
Calprotectin is for IBD versus IBS.
Scoping now risks perforation and sees only the left colon.
A cancer can mimic diverticulitis; the colon must be checked.

steps.x: **A. Colonoscopy in about 6 weeks.** Rule: CT acutely, scope later.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has 2 days of left iliac fossa pain. He is eating and drinking. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. He has mild left iliac fossa tenderness without guarding. CT shows uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild uncomplicated diverticulitis with significant comorbidity: oral co-amoxiclav, simple analgesia and safety-netting. He does not need admission.

steps.x: Initial management: decide home or hospital, then antibiotics or not.

clues: type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease
steps.x: Well enough for home, but comorbidity makes antibiotics indicated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral co-amoxiclav**, paracetamol, fluids, safety-net.

elim: He is not systemically unwell enough for IV treatment.
No perforation or peritonitis.
Metronidazole alone misses Gram-negative cover.
Colonoscopy is avoided acutely.

steps.x: **C. Oral co-amoxiclav and paracetamol.** Rule: co-amoxiclav covers Gram-negatives and anaerobes.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with diverticular disease has a 12 hour history of generalised abdominal pain. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. Her abdomen is rigid. CT shows free intraperitoneal gas and faecal contamination arising from a perforated sigmoid colon. She has been resuscitated with IV fluids and antibiotics.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Perforated diverticulitis with faecal peritonitis needs Hartmann's procedure. Percutaneous drainage only treats a contained abscess.

steps.x: Definitive management of a perforated, contaminated abdomen.

clues: free intraperitoneal gas and faecal contamination
steps.x: Faecal peritonitis and septic shock from the sigmoid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resect the sigmoid with an end colostomy: **Hartmann's procedure**.

elim: Drainage is for a contained abscess, not free faecal peritonitis.
Antibiotics alone cannot control faecal soiling.
She is in septic shock; oral treatment is unsafe.
The disease is in the sigmoid, not the right colon.

steps.x: **B. Hartmann's procedure.** Rule: faecal peritonitis = resect and stoma.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman has intermittent left lower abdominal cramps and bloating. A recent colonoscopy showed sigmoid diverticula only. She has been constipated for years and eats little fruit or vegetables. She has no fever or rectal bleeding. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Diverticular disease is managed first with more dietary fibre, hydration and treating constipation. A low-residue diet would worsen constipation.

steps.x: First-line management of symptomatic but non-inflamed diverticula.
Diverticular disease driven by constipation and low fibre.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Increase fibre and fluids**, manage constipation.

elim: Surgery is not for uncomplicated symptomatic disease.
No infection to treat.
Low residue worsens constipation.
Mesalazine is for ulcerative colitis.

steps.x: **B. Increase dietary fibre and fluids.**

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with sigmoid diverticulosis develops acute left iliac fossa pain and fever. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. CT confirms acute diverticulitis. The surgeon explains that a hard plug of stool was likely responsible for starting the inflammation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his acute illness?
o: Autoimmune inflammation of the colonic mucosa
Bacterial overgrowth behind a faecolith blocking a diverticulum
Torsion of the sigmoid on its mesentery
practice.e: A faecolith obstructs a diverticulum, causing bacterial overgrowth, inflammation and micro-perforation. Granulomatous transmural inflammation is Crohn's disease.

steps.x: Mechanism of diverticulitis.
A plug of stool = faecolith blocking the neck of a pouch.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Obstruction by a **faecolith** → bacterial overgrowth → inflammation.

elim: Autoimmune mucosal inflammation is ulcerative colitis.
Granulomas are Crohn's disease.
Low-flow ischaemia is ischaemic colitis.
Torsion is volvulus.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: diverticulitis is a blocked pouch, like a mini appendicitis.
